question:
For an all-or-nothing vaccine, will the 1-incidence rate ratio overestimate / underestimate / correctly estimate the per-exposure vaccine efficacy?

Answer Choices:
A. overestimate
B. underestimate
C. correctly estimate
D. /
E. /

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine (fraction p fully protected at 100% efficacy; fraction 1-p fully unprotected), the force of infection among remaining susceptibles is identical in both arms. The observed incidence rate ratio therefore begins at 1-p but increases toward 1 over time because the protected individuals no longer contribute events while the unprotected continue to experience the same hazard as the unvaccinated. Consequently 1-IRR is biased upward relative to the true proportion protected and underestimates per-exposure vaccine efficacy. 

B. underestimate

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The 1-IRR will underestimate the target quantity (B).  

An all-or-nothing vaccine partitions the vaccinated cohort into a completely protected fraction \(\varepsilon\) (hazard 0) and an unprotected fraction \(1-\varepsilon\) (hazard identical to the unvaccinated). In the absence of depletion the person-time incidence rate in the vaccinated arm is therefore exactly \((1-\varepsilon)\lambda\), the IRR equals \(1-\varepsilon\), and \(1-\text{IRR}=\varepsilon\).  

Once exposures accumulate, however, the higher-risk individuals are preferentially removed from the unvaccinated arm. Consequently the observed (average) IRR rises above \(1-\varepsilon\), so that \(1-\text{IRR}<\varepsilon\). The quantity recovered from incidence rates therefore systematically understates the all-or-nothing efficacy parameter. (The bias is the mirror image of the well-known over-estimation that occurs with a leaky vaccine under the same conditions.)  

This reasoning uses only the standard susceptible-depletion argument and does not rely on any external sources.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the answer is B. underestimate. For an all-or-nothing vaccine, the people who are fully protected never contribute any events, so the observed incidence in the vaccinated arm is driven only by the unprotected fraction. When you compute 1 minus the incidence rate ratio, that effectively averages the zero efficacy in the protected group with the full susceptibility in the unprotected group, but because the rate ratio is taken over the whole population denominator it ends up shrinking the apparent protection relative to the true per-exposure efficacy among those who remain susceptible. That dilution should push the estimate downward.

10.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I lean toward B. underestimate. For an all-or-nothing vaccine the 1-IRR is computed from aggregate incidence over the full follow-up period, which mixes protected and unprotected individuals and therefore dilutes the per-exposure protection that would be observed if we could isolate only the exposures occurring in the vaccinated group; the resulting bias is downward relative to the true per-exposure VE.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine, a fraction p of recipients receive complete (100%) protection while the remainder receive none. This implies that the per-exposure infection hazard in the vaccinated group is exactly (1-p) times the unvaccinated hazard. Consequently the incidence rate ratio equals 1-p, so 1-IRR recovers p exactly and therefore equals the average per-exposure vaccine efficacy. The estimate is unbiased (C).

(The contrast case is a leaky vaccine, where the same 1-IRR underestimates the per-exposure efficacy because the hazards are no longer proportional once conditioning on survival.)

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine, a fraction \(p\) of recipients receive complete (sterilizing) protection while the remainder receive none. Under a constant force of infection \(\lambda\), the observed incidence rate among vaccinees is therefore exactly \((1-p)\lambda\). The incidence rate ratio is consequently \(1-p\) at every instant, so \(1-\text{IRR}=p\) recovers the proportion protected without bias. Because the per-exposure efficacy for the protected individuals is 1 (and 0 for the unprotected), the population-level quantity estimated by \(1-\text{IRR}\) equals the average per-exposure efficacy; hence the estimator is unbiased. The answer is therefore C.

(The same algebra shows that a leaky vaccine, in which every individual experiences the identical per-exposure reduction \(1-\text{VE}\), likewise yields an unbiased IRR-based estimator; the distinction between the two modes of action appears only when secondary attack rates or time-varying hazards are examined.)

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p of recipients are fully protected (per-exposure efficacy = 1) and the remainder have zero protection. Under constant exposure the force of infection therefore acts only on the (1-p) susceptible fraction of the vaccinated cohort. Because susceptibles are depleted faster among the unvaccinated, the observed person-time incidence rate ratio rises toward 1 over follow-up; consequently its time-averaged value exceeds (1-p). Thus 1-IRR understates the true proportion protected (i.e., the per-exposure vaccine efficacy). The correct choice is therefore B.

(The result is the mirror image of the “leaky” case, in which 1-IRR is unbiased for the constant per-exposure efficacy.)

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine (fraction p fully protected with 100% per-exposure protection; fraction 1-p unaffected), the incidence rate among vaccinated individuals equals exactly (1-p) times the incidence rate among unvaccinated individuals at every moment, assuming the same underlying force of infection acting on the susceptible pool. Consequently the incidence rate ratio remains constantly equal to 1-p, so that 1-IRR exactly recovers the proportion protected (i.e., the per-exposure vaccine efficacy averaged across the vaccinated cohort). The estimator is therefore unbiased.

Thus the answer is C. correctly estimate.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The 1-IRR from an all-or-nothing vaccine will overestimate per-exposure VE (A). 

Reasoning: An all-or-nothing vaccine fully protects a fraction ε of recipients and leaves the remainder fully susceptible. The resulting hazards are non-proportional; the unprotected fraction is depleted faster than the unvaccinated cohort, so the time-averaged incidence rate among the vaccinated is lower than the constant rate (1-ε)λ that would be observed under proportional hazards. Consequently the observed IRR falls below 1-ε, which means 1-IRR > ε. The quantity ε is precisely the average per-exposure efficacy, so the 1-IRR estimate is biased upward. (By contrast, a leaky vaccine produces constant proportional hazards and the 1-IRR recovers the per-exposure efficacy without bias.)

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The key distinction here is between an all-or-nothing vaccine (a fraction p of recipients acquire complete immunity; the remainder acquire none) versus a leaky vaccine. Per-exposure vaccine efficacy is the proportionate reduction in infection hazard on each exposure (i.e., the average susceptibility parameter across the vaccinated cohort).  

Under a constant force of infection λ, the incidence rate among unvaccinated subjects is exactly λ, because person-time accrues only while subjects remain susceptible. Among vaccinated subjects the incidence rate is strictly lower than λ(1−p) because the fully immune fraction contributes extra person-time without ever becoming cases. Consequently the observed incidence-rate ratio is smaller than 1−p, so 1−IRR > p. The incidence-rate estimator therefore overestimates the true per-exposure efficacy parameter.  

(This bias is the mirror image of the well-known result for leaky vaccines, where 1−IRR recovers the per-exposure efficacy exactly.)  

Thus the correct choice is A.  

(The result can be verified algebraically from the expressions for cumulative cases and person-time over any finite follow-up interval T.)
